deck.title: Talksmith Style Reference
deck.class: One example of every slide template, plus layout edge cases

slides.title: Frames & openers
This deck renders one example of every Talksmith slide template.
slides.sub: Flip through it, or diff style-reference.html, and any styling regression jumps out.

slides.title: A divider is a plain sub-opener within a section
Statement & emphasis
A statement slide is one dominant claim, set large.
slides.sub: No bullets, no cards — just the single line you want the room to remember.

slides.title: A statement title can run long, and it should still wrap gracefully across two or three lines while reading as one strong, uninterrupted assertion.
big-number: one hero metric
slides.caption: big-number is for a single hero figure — one number set very large, one caption, nothing competing with it.

slides.quote: A quote slide is the whole slide — one voiced line, centered, with an attribution beneath.
No hubo hackers. No hubo malware. Alguien pegó código en un chatbot.
slides.notes: A quote with no attribution. Plenty of quoted lines have no person to name — a slogan, an anonymized line from a user interview, a sentence from a standard or a report, something said in the room. The template treats attribution as optional and renders nothing in its place: the quotation mark and the centering already say these are someone else's words, which is the only thing that distinguishes a quote from a statement. The rule this fixture guards is that the fill must not invent an attribution to satisfy the template, and must not demote the slide to statement because none exists.

slides.title: callout: an emphasized aside

callout.label: Think of it this way
callout.body: A callout is a single rounded panel for a tip, analogy, or warning — pink for a lateral note, blue for a declarative takeaway.

slides.title: callout: the blue tone

callout.label: The other tone
callout.body: Blue is the declarative takeaway — a conclusion the audience should carry out of the slide. Pink (previous slide) is the lateral note: an aside, analogy, or caution.

slides.title: single-point: one lead plus one point

point.label: The rule
point.body: When a slide is a claim plus exactly one supporting beat, give that beat a card — never a lone bullet floating under a title.

slides.title: Enumerations
concept-breakdown: 2 cards, explicit icons, reveal together

cards.label: Two is valid
cards.body: A two-item labeled set is a real concept-breakdown, not something to drop to prose.

cards.label: Iconed
cards.body: Each card still gets its own distinct, content-matched icon beside the label.

slides.title: concept-breakdown: 3 cards (2 + 1 across the width)

cards.label: Unordered
cards.body: The cards have no sequence; order carries no meaning here.

cards.label: Short bodies
cards.body: Keep each body to a line or two so the grid stays even.

cards.label: No source image
cards.body: Any picture would route the slide to figures instead.

slides.title: concept-breakdown: 4 cards (2×2), longer bodies edge case

cards.label: Capacity
cards.body: Two through six cards fit; beyond six, split across two slides so nothing has to shrink.

cards.label: Wrapping
cards.body: Longer bodies wrap inside their card, and all four cards hold the same height as a 2×2 grid.

cards.label: Distinct icons
cards.body: The renderer never repeats an icon within a slide, so four cards means four different glyphs.

cards.label: When to switch
cards.body: If a body is too long to read comfortably here, move it to icon-list, which gives each row prose room.

slides.title: concept-breakdown: 6 cards (3×2), the dense edge

cards.label: Default home
cards.body: The general case for any labeled set of two or more.

cards.label: Grid
cards.body: Six cards lay out as a 3×2 grid with uniform gutters.

cards.label: Icon each
cards.body: Six distinct icons, one anchoring every concept.

cards.label: Terse
cards.body: At six cards, keep every body to a single short line.

cards.label: Split point
cards.body: Need more than six? Split the set across two slides.

cards.label: Still cards
cards.body: Even this dense, it is cards — never a bullet list.

slides.title: concept-breakdown · editorial: 3 concepts, one row of three
slides.lead: The editorial format keeps the icon, the label and the body, and drops the panel around them:

cards.label: No card
cards.body: No fill, no radius, no wide padding — the concept sits on the canvas.

cards.label: Small icon
cards.body: The glyph is a reference mark beside the label, not the anchor.

cards.label: One row
cards.body: Three concepts share a single row instead of two plus one wide.

slides.title: concept-breakdown · editorial: 4 concepts, a 2×2 grid
slides.lead: Four concepts fill two columns over two rows — the same rhythm the card grid uses, without the boxes:

cards.label: Two columns
cards.body: Each concept takes half the useful width, so the measure stays comfortable.

cards.label: Aligned labels
cards.body: Labels in a row share a baseline; bodies indent to the label's left edge.

cards.label: A hairline, not a box
cards.body: One thin rule marks the row; white space does the rest of the separating.

cards.label: Opt-in
cards.body: Set format editorial; leaving it off keeps the card grid exactly as it was.

slides.title: concept-breakdown · editorial: 5 concepts, three then two centered
slides.lead: A short last row keeps the width of the row above and centers, instead of stretching to fill:

cards.label: Three up top
cards.body: The first row sets the column rhythm.

cards.label: Same width
cards.body: Row two keeps that item width, so every measure matches.

cards.label: Centered
cards.body: The leftover width splits evenly on both sides.

cards.label: Never one wide
cards.body: No item ever spans a whole row on its own.

cards.label: Room to breathe
cards.body: The unused half-columns read as white space, not as a gap.

slides.title: concept-breakdown · editorial: 6 concepts, a 3×2 grid
slides.lead: Six concepts are the format's comfortable middle — three columns over two rows:

cards.label: Three columns
cards.body: The same span as the three-concept row, twice over.

cards.label: Even density
cards.body: Six flat blocks weigh less than six cards.

cards.label: Rows read across
cards.body: Reading order stays left to right, top to bottom.

cards.label: Short bodies
cards.body: Around a hundred characters each at this width.

cards.label: Longer prose warns
cards.body: The build says so instead of shrinking the type.

cards.label: Or use list
cards.body: The vertical format has the room prose needs.

slides.title: concept-breakdown · editorial: 7 concepts, four then three centered
slides.lead: Seven is the count the card grid handled worst — 3+3+1 left a single item stranded on its own row:

cards.label: Four up top
cards.body: Seven and eight concepts move to four columns.

cards.label: Type steps down
cards.body: Icon and text shrink one notch at four across.

cards.label: Three centered
cards.body: The second row centers on the same grid.

cards.label: No orphan row
cards.body: Nothing is left alone across the width.

cards.label: Keep bodies short
cards.body: Roughly seventy characters at this width.

cards.label: Still legible
cards.body: The step-down is bounded, not open-ended.

cards.label: Past that, split
cards.body: Two slides beat one unreadable one.

slides.title: concept-breakdown · editorial: 8 concepts, a 4×2 grid
slides.lead: Eight is the ceiling — a regular four-by-two grid, with the takeaway kept out of it:

cards.label: Four by two
cards.body: A regular grid, no partial row.

cards.label: Equal widths
cards.body: Every concept gets the same measure.

cards.label: Row rules
cards.body: Hairlines mark the two rows.

cards.label: Small glyphs
cards.body: Icons support, they do not lead.

cards.label: Aligned
cards.body: Labels in a row share a baseline.

cards.label: White space
cards.body: The row gap carries the separation.

cards.label: Scans fast
cards.body: Eight flat blocks stay readable.

cards.label: The ceiling
cards.body: A ninth concept means a second slide.

highlights.body: A conclusion stays a full-width band under the grid — it is a comment on the set, never a ninth cell in it.

slides.title: aside: a full-bleed image column on the right
slides.lead: The image reinforces the point; the text carries it.

image.alt: An abstract texture standing in for an atmospheric photo

slides.notes: The aside is the slide-model expression of an author's `<!-- aside: ... -->` hint in draft.md. It reserves roughly 37% of the slide width as a full-bleed image column and pads the stage on that side so the head and body lay out in what remains. Because the column crops to fill rather than fitting the whole image, it is only ever atmosphere: a diagram, chart, or screenshot the audience must actually read belongs in a template that owns its image, where it is contained and legible.

cards.label: Atmosphere, not information
cards.body: The column crops to fill, so nothing in it needs to be read closely.

cards.label: Default side
cards.body: An aside sits on the right unless the hint says left.

cards.label: Any stage-based type
cards.body: The stage macro adds it, so every content template supports it.

slides.title: aside: the same column, on the left

cards.label: side: left
cards.body: The hint's optional side moves the column to the other edge.

cards.label: Content reflows
cards.body: The stage pads whichever side the image takes.

image.alt: An abstract texture standing in for an atmospheric photo

slides.notes: The left variant exists for rhythm: alternating the side across a run of slides keeps a deck from feeling like a template. The choice carries no semantics — it is purely visual pacing.

slides.title: card-row: 3 short cards with a lead
slides.lead: A lead line sits above a single horizontal row of three to five short cards:

cards.label: Lead
cards.body: One framing sentence introduces the row.

cards.label: Short
cards.body: Each body stays under about eighty characters.

cards.label: One row
cards.body: Three to five cards share one horizontal band.

slides.title: Legacy `icon-list` → the card grid
slides.lead: The retired `list` format stacked these in one column; the legacy id now renders them as **cards**:

rows.label: Parallel reads side by side
rows.body: A labeled set is N *peers*. Stacking them spent the whole slide width on one item and made the set read as a sequence.

rows.label: The lead survives
rows.body: `grid` carries the lead the retired format carried, so nothing an old model wrote is dropped on the way over.

rows.label: Prose still fits
rows.body: A card holds up to about two sentences. Past that the slide is not a labeled set — it is `content-text`, or two slides.

slides.title: A bare anaphora → label-only cards

rows.label: Each parallel line becomes one card.
This keeps such slides off the fallback path.

slides.title: Inline styling works in *every* field
slides.lead: `**bold**`, `*italic*`, `~~strike~~`, `` `code` ``, `[text](url)` and a naked URL are resolved in **every** text field of **every** template:

cards.label: **Bold** a figure
cards.body: Entrenar un LMM puede consumir **700.000 litros** de agua — the number carries the line, so it reads as the number.

cards.label: *Italic* a term
cards.body: The *lead* is the title's sub-line; the *body* is what follows it.

cards.label: `code` inline
cards.body: A field name like `slide-model.json` or a flag like `--print-pdf` keeps the mono face, and **a `.md` file named inside a bolded phrase** stays bold across it.

cards.label: ~~Strike~~ a superseded value
cards.body: A figure the slide corrects reads ~~1.2M~~ **4.4M** — struck, not deleted, so the correction is visible.

cards.label: A titled [link](https://www.who.int)
cards.body: `[text](url)` shows the title and hides the address. Only `http:`, `https:` and `mailto:` link — `[x](javascript:…)` stays literal text.

cards.label: URLs link themselves
cards.body: Raw as https://www.who.int/data, the angle form <https://who.int>, www.who.int/es, and even schemeless — app.sli.do/event/x — all become clickable. The trailing period stays outside.

highlights.body: Fuente: [WHO — Ethics and governance of AI for health](https://www.who.int) (2024) — dudas a [este correo](mailto:deck@example.org).

slides.notes:
Inline styling is resolved once, in html_style.py `_richtext`/`_inline_md`, on the slide's prose fields — not per template — so any field of any template accepts the marks. Escaping runs first, so authored HTML in a field stays inert text; code blocks, image paths and the enum-ish fields the renderer branches on are excluded, because their bytes are the content.

Speaker notes take the same grammar (this note is proof: **bold** resolves here too) plus their own line breaks, because notes are prose the presenter reads rather than a schema field.

The grammar stops at inline marks on purpose: block markdown inside a field (headings, lists, tables) would let content route around the schema, which is where the template and its fields do their work.

slides.title: Ordered & comparison
process: an ordered sequence of steps
slides.lead: Use process when order carries meaning — steps, phases, or a numbered flow:

steps.label: Classify
steps.body: The fill step reads final.md and picks each slide's template.

steps.label: Decompose
steps.body: It splits the body into that template's exact required fields.

steps.label: Render
steps.body: build_html.py maps those fields onto Jinja templates, mechanically.

slides.title: A plain enumeration → the numbered list
slides.lead: Seven unlabeled lines: no labels to card up, so they number instead of falling to bullets.

steps.body: Uno cada dos clases, relacionado con temas vistos.
En grupos de 2 personas.
Valen **40%** de la nota final.
Gran parte del trabajo se completa en clase.
Entrega: antes del viernes siguiente vía repositorio GitHub.
Todos los entregables son obligatorios.
Entregas tardías impactan la nota.

slides.notes: A list whose items carry no label has nothing to build a card around, so it used to land on fallback and draw as bare bullets. It belongs on process instead: the unlabeled branch of that template is already a numbered list — an outlined number chip and the line — and the numbering is what earns the slide. It turns a loose list into a countable set the audience can hold in mind and the presenter can point at, without implying the items are steps in a sequence. The single column is deliberate here, unlike the labeled set: a numbered list is read top to bottom, and splitting it across columns breaks the count.

slides.title: process: plain numbered steps
slides.lead: When the steps are ordered but unlabeled, render them as a vertical numbered list:

steps.body: Identify the data you are about to share and where it came from.
Classify its sensitivity before it leaves your workspace.
Choose an approved tool for that classification.
Record what was shared so the workflow can be audited later.

slides.title: concept-columns: four terms, the third emphasised
slides.lead: Each column explains its own term; reading across a row says nothing.

columns.label: Language Model
columns.body: Asigna probabilidades a secuencias de palabras: dado un contexto, predice qué sigue.

columns.label: Foundation Model
columns.body: Entrenado a escala masiva sobre datos generales, adaptable a múltiples tareas.

columns.label: LLM
columns.body: Un Foundation Model especializado en texto: aprende la distribución del lenguaje natural.

columns.label: Modelo Multimodal
columns.body: Un Foundation Model que procesa y genera varios tipos de dato a la vez.
text: Un solo modelo para ver, oír y hablar

highlights.label: Relación
highlights.body: Todo LLM es un Foundation Model, pero no todo Foundation Model es un LLM.

slides.notes: Four terms explained side by side. The columns deliberately share no row structure — that is the whole discriminator against value-columns, which is a table wearing columns and whose cells align row by row against a shared factor. Here reading across a row says nothing: each column is read top to bottom on its own, and one column may carry four bullets where its neighbour carries a paragraph. The emphasised column marks the term the slide is about, the one the others define by contrast; it is not a verdict, so the older or worse option may carry it just as well.

slides.title: concept-columns: two terms, no shared factors
slides.lead: It looks adversarial, but there is no row to read across — so it is not a comparison grid.

columns.label: IA Tradicional
columns.body: Un modelo por tarea específica, entrenado en casa.
columns.example: Ejemplo: un detector de fallos en autopartes sólo detecta eso.
text: Requiere datos etiquetados abundantes para cada caso de uso
Difícil de reutilizar entre dominios distintos

columns.label: Foundation Models
columns.body: Modelos entrenados con datos a gran escala que adquieren una comprensión general y se adaptan después.
columns.text:
Se exponen como SaaS o se pueden correr localmente.
No hace falta un equipo de data science para empezar a usarlos.

highlights.body: Lectura recomendada: [On the Opportunities and Risks of Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.07258) (Stanford HAI, 2021).

slides.notes: The two-column case, and the one most likely to be misclassified. It reads adversarial — old way versus new way — but there is no shared factor and no row to read across, so it is not a value-columns grid: each side is explained in its own terms, with its own internal structure. Note also that the emphasised column here is the traditional approach, not the one the talk advocates: emphasis marks the subject under discussion, never the winner.

slides.title: design: split-right — media contained on the right
slides.lead: A diagram the audience actually reads gets half the canvas, uncropped.

cards.label: Design first
cards.body: How the canvas is divided is chosen before the template.

cards.label: Style second
cards.body: The template only says what shape the content takes.

slides.notes: Design and style are separate decisions, so they are separate fields. The stage places `media` per `design`; the template emits content and nothing else. That is why every content template accepts every design — the old `layout` field existed on five templates only, and `aside` was a second vocabulary for the same decision, so a template on neither list could not be composed at all. This slide is a `concept-breakdown`, a template that could never carry a composed image before.

highlights.body: Fuente: [WHO — Ethics and governance of AI for health](https://www.who.int) (2024).

This slide is a `concept-breakdown`, a template that could never carry a composed image before.

slides.title: video: a clip is media — split-right, contained
slides.notes: A clip on a slide is a demo recording: it runs while the presenter narrates over it. Because the video carries the point and the PDF export only prints its first frame, whatever it shows has to be said here too — a reader of the deck never sees it move.

cards.label: Autoplays
cards.body: Reveal starts it when the slide comes up and pauses it on the way out.

cards.label: Same frame
cards.body: A video takes the box an image would, in every design.

slides.title: video: cropped to fill — column-right
slides.notes: The column design crops media to fill its strip, which for video means the same rule as for a photo: nothing load-bearing goes in it. Ambient motion behind a text slide is what this is for — muted and looping, so it never ends mid-talk and never competes with the presenter's voice.

cards.label: Atmosphere
cards.body: A column crops to fill, so nothing in the clip is meant to be read.

cards.label: Looping
cards.body: muted + loop is the shape ambient motion takes: it cycles, quietly.

slides.title: A source pins to the bottom edge
slides.lead: This slide is deliberately short.

point.label: Chrome, not a remark
point.body: The citation credits the material; it does not comment on it, so it leaves the content flow entirely.

highlights.body: A takeaway *is* a remark on the body, so it stays with the body.
Fuente: [OMS — Ethics and governance of AI for health](https://www.who.int) (2024).

slides.notes: A source highlight is emitted as a child of the stage rather than of .cfit, so it is pinned to the slide's bottom edge instead of trailing the content wherever the content happens to end. Two consequences follow from that placement, and both are the reason for it: on a short slide the citation stays on the baseline instead of floating up under a half-empty body, and the per-slide content-fit pass — which only ever scales .cfit — can neither shrink it nor move it. Every other highlight kind is a remark on the body and stays inside .cfit, where it moves and scales with what it remarks on.

Quiz
slides.question: In a Talksmith quiz slide, when does the answer appear?
slides.answer: On next-nav — the question shows first so the audience can think, then the answer fades up.
slides.explanation: The correct choice highlights in sync; space is reserved so the question never jumps.
slides.notes: Let the room commit to an answer before you advance; the reveal is one navigation step away.

slides.title: Quiz with a supporting image
slides.question: Where does a quiz slide put its image?
slides.answer: Beside the quiz — contained, sized to its own aspect.
slides.explanation: The quiz body and the image split the slide; the image is never cropped.

slides.title: matrix: cells indexed by two named axes
slides.lead: A quadrant is not four cards — a cell means what it means because of where it sits.

cells.label: True positive
cells.body: Called it, and it was there.

cells.label: False negative
cells.body: Missed it. The expensive one in medicine.

cells.label: False positive
cells.body: False alarm. The expensive one in spam.

slides.notes: A matrix earns its own template because the axes carry meaning. Filed as four concept cards, the labels survive and the axes vanish — and the axes were the point. The tone colours reuse the pros-cons pair rather than introducing a third palette.

slides.title: media as a code panel — cards keep their cards

media.code:

scaler.fit(X_train)            # train only
X_val  = scaler.transform(X_val)
X_test = scaler.transform(X_test)

cards.label: Learned from train
cards.body: The statistics come from one split and one split only.

cards.label: Applied to all three
cards.body: Same parameters, every time — that is what makes it a transform.

cards.label: Silent when wrong
cards.body: Leak the test set in and nothing raises; the score just flatters you.

slides.notes: Before media could hold code, this slide had two bad options: drop the snippet to keep the cards, or become a code-example and flatten the cards into an explanation column. Both lose content. The design places the panel; the template still just emits cards.

cards.body: The one that always works, and the one nobody has.

slides.notes: A lookup table is supporting evidence here, not the slide — so it rides in media like a diagram would. Rendered with the same compare-strip classes value-columns uses, so a table beside a body and a table that is the body read as one piece.

slides.title: a stat band under the body
slides.lead: Two figures that comment on the body — without making the whole slide a stat.

facts.label: The hook is a contrast
facts.body: A pair of numbers can carry a slide's opening without being its structure.

slides.notes: The catalog always described a stat pair as the lower band of a content slide, but only the stat template had a stats field — so a slide with this hook had to become a stat and demote its cards. The band is now universal; stat is for when the numbers are the whole slide.
